story.headline: Russian mass strike kills 15 across Ukraine
story.summary: Russia's overnight missile and drone attack on 7 October killed at least 15 people across Ukraine.
story.display_body: Russia launched another mass missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities overnight into Wednesday 7 October, killing at least 15 people and wounding more than 40. The deadliest strike hit a five-storey apartment block in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, killing at least nine people, three of them children, and wounding 38, the Kyiv Independent reported. Two people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district, and Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Oleksandriya and Zaporizhzhia were also hit. According to Ukraine's Air Force, Russia fired 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles; it said 117 drones and 39 cruise missiles were shot down or jammed. Volodymyr Zelensky called it "one of the most perfidious attacks" and said the army had "offered" the destroyed homes to Vladimir Putin for his 74th birthday, which fell on Wednesday. Zelensky had warned on Tuesday 6 October that a mass strike was being prepared.
story.why: the attack shows Russia keeps the capacity to fire dozens of missiles in a single night as winter approaches, which keeps pressure on Ukraine's air defences and on the allies who supply them.

story.headline: US presses Russia over Siberia plague scare
story.summary: The US asked Russia for more information on a suspected pneumonic plague death at an Irkutsk research institute.
story.display_body: The United States has formally asked Russia for "more information" about the death of a laboratory technician at a plague research institute in Siberia, which has raised fears of a case of pneumonic plague (the lung form of the disease, which spreads between people). The worker, Darya Shipilova, was employed at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov. Independent Russian media reported that she may have broken a test tube containing plague bacteria at work on Friday 25 September, but Russian authorities have not confirmed this account. Russian officials deny that any anti-plague measures are in place, and Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said on Monday 5 October that the sanitary situation was stable. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday 6 October that it was "incumbent upon Russia" to share more with the world. Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and can be treated with antibiotics if caught early.
story.why: no laboratory has publicly confirmed plague, so the case is still unverified; the open question is whether Moscow will share test results under international health rules, which would allow an independent assessment of the risk.

story.headline: Houthis target Aden airport and Riyadh
story.summary: The Houthis fired missiles at Aden airport and toward Riyadh on 7 October amid Yemen's government offensive.
story.display_body: Yemen's government said the Houthis fired at least two ballistic missiles and several drones at Aden International Airport on Wednesday 7 October, and Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh. One missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land; the flight was diverted to Jeddah, and two aircraft were moved off the tarmac, according to the Yemeni Transport Ministry. The Houthis said they had targeted "Saudi military supplies" at a camp near the airport. They also claimed drone attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha, which Saudi authorities have not confirmed. The Saudi-led coalition said it had traced the Riyadh launch to Houthi-held Sanaa and would destroy the launcher. The strikes come three days after the government launched its offensive on Sunday 4 October to retake Houthi-held territory, and government forces have since pushed the Houthis back around the Bab al-Mandeb strait and Mocha.
story.why: attacks on civilian airports in Aden and the Saudi capital spread the renewed war beyond the front lines, and the Houthis are showing they can still hit Saudi Arabia while losing ground on the coast.

story.headline: Mali army retakes Kidal as separatists withdraw
story.summary: Mali's army and Russian forces entered Kidal on 6 October after FLA separatists withdrew.
story.display_body: Mali's army and its Russian partners entered the northern town of Kidal on the afternoon of Tuesday 6 October, after the separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) withdrew without a fight. The FLA and the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM had seized Kidal in April, in attacks that also killed Mali's defence minister. The general staff said it had launched "large-scale air-land operations" in the region with its "Russian partners". The FLA called its exit a temporary "strategic withdrawal" meant to protect the few civilians still in the town, and blamed what it called the "disproportionate use of aerial assets" by the Russian Africa Corps. An analyst at Control Risks told Reuters the recapture was largely "symbolic" rather than "decisive".
story.why: retaking Kidal is a boost for a military government that relies on Russian paramilitaries after several recent setbacks, but the armed groups have pulled back rather than been defeated.

story.headline: AfD wins first German state speakership
story.summary: Saxony-Anhalt's parliament elected the AfD's Tobias Rausch as its president on 6 October.
story.display_body: Saxony-Anhalt's new state parliament elected Tobias Rausch of the AfD as its president on Tuesday 6 October, the first time since the Second World War that a German state parliament has chosen a speaker from a party the domestic intelligence service classifies as right-wing extremist. Rausch received 48 votes, nine more than the AfD has seats, DW reported. SRF noted that this was four votes more than the AfD's own seats plus those the BSW had already promised him. The 35-year-old is best known for his role in a nepotism affair over relatives and associates employed in AfD offices. The session was opened by its oldest member, Eva von Angern of the Left Party, who quoted the Basic Law's guarantee of human dignity.
story.why: the AfD hopes that votes from beyond its own group could one day bring it the state premiership, and this vote shows that such support exists.

story.headline: Kosovo elects president, averting snap election
story.summary: Kosovo's parliament elected Justina Shiroka-Pula president on 6 October, avoiding dissolution.
story.display_body: Kosovo's parliament elected economist Justina Shiroka-Pula as president just before midnight on Tuesday 6 October, avoiding the dissolution of parliament and what would have been a fourth parliamentary election in less than two years. Shiroka-Pula received 81 votes, and two ballots were invalid. Prime Minister Albin Kurti nominated her at a late-evening press conference after the opposition PDK had rejected earlier candidates. A former energy minister (2008–2011) and former PDK MP, she has headed Kosovo's Academy of Sciences and Arts since December 2025, and she is the country's third woman president. The deadlock had become tied up with demands to curb the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which last month convicted four former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders of war crimes.
story.why: the vote ends months of institutional paralysis, but the dispute over the war-crimes court is still unresolved.

story.headline: Swiss jobless rate holds at 3%
story.summary: Swiss unemployment held at 3.0% in September; unemployment insurance posted a 2025 loss after a federal contribution cut.
story.display_body: Swiss unemployment held at 3.0% in September, but the number of jobless people was 5.4% higher than a year earlier, SECO reported on Tuesday 6 October. There were 140,480 registered unemployed people, and the seasonally adjusted rate stayed at 3.1%. Jobseekers, a broader measure that also counts people in training programmes or temporary work, numbered 227,592 (4.8%). Job vacancies reported to regional placement offices were up 18.3% on the year. In Vaud the rate stayed at 4.9%, against 4.5% a year earlier; the canton says it would be 4.5% if, like most cantons, it did not count people whose benefits have run out. SECO also published the 2025 accounts of the unemployment insurance fund, which show a loss of CHF 249 million after a CHF 1.43 billion surplus in 2024. SECO attributes the loss mainly to the federal budget relief law: it scrapped the Confederation's whole 2025 contribution of about CHF 600 million, as part of CHF 1.25 billion in cuts for 2025–2029, at a time when spending rose with unemployment.
story.why: the fund's loss comes mainly from the federal cut rather than the labour market alone, which matters as unemployment drifts upward.

story.headline: Tamedia cuts 34 newsroom posts
story.summary: Tamedia announced 34 newsroom job cuts on 6 October; Vaud's government voiced concern for Romandy's press.
story.display_body: Tamedia announced on Tuesday 6 October that it will cut 34 full-time newsroom posts, affecting 41 people, and Vaud's Council of State said it was "deeply worried" about Romandy's media. According to the Vaud government, 28 of those affected work in German-speaking newsrooms and 9 in French-speaking Switzerland. The cuts come less than two weeks after Ringier announced 14 job cuts in Lausanne on 23 September, including six in the newsrooms of Blick Romandie, L'illustré and PME. The Council of State said it would make sure the consultation procedure that has now opened complies with the law, and it warned of a "real risk" that the region's press will be weakened.
story.why: this is the third round of newsroom cuts announced in a few weeks, and the French-speaking regional titles that cover local politics in Vaud are again among those affected.

story.headline: Nuclear-ban referendum filed in Bern
story.summary: Opponents filed over 131,800 signatures for a referendum against new Swiss nuclear plants on 6 October.
story.display_body: An alliance of the SP, the Greens, the GLP and parts of the Centre party filed its referendum against new nuclear power plants in Bern on Tuesday 6 October, with more than 131,800 signatures by its own count. The referendum targets Parliament's decision to lift Switzerland's ban on building new reactors, which was passed as an indirect counter-proposal to the "Stop the blackout" initiative. If the Federal Chancellery confirms that it has qualified, the vote could be held on Sunday 28 February 2027 at the earliest. Supporters of lifting the ban point out that nuclear plants supply almost 30% of domestic electricity and say they are needed for winter supply. Opponents say new reactors would divert money from renewables, and the GLP wants solar subsidies protected.
story.why: voters, not Parliament, will now have the final say on whether new reactors can be built in Switzerland.

story.headline: Swiss army headcount set to shrink
story.summary: The Swiss army counted 147,017 soldiers in 2026 but expects fewer than 130,000 by 2030.
story.display_body: The Swiss army had 147,017 soldiers assigned to units as of 1 March 2026, but the number is likely to fall below 130,000 by 2030, the Defence Department said on Tuesday 6 October. The current number is enough to guarantee the legal minimum of 100,000 troops in an emergency. The drop comes after the last two age groups that served 12 years of compulsory service are released in 2028 and 2029. Fitness for service stands at 70%, and the share of women continues to rise slowly. A mandatory information day for women, which the Federal Council sent to Parliament in September, could go to a popular vote around 2028.
story.why: keeping the army at full strength is becoming a long-term problem just as defence spending and readiness move up the political agenda.

story.headline: Geneva initiative seeks vote on CERN collider
story.summary: A Geneva initiative was launched to guarantee a popular vote on CERN's Future Circular Collider.
story.display_body: A coalition of Geneva associations launched a cantonal initiative on Tuesday 6 October to guarantee a popular vote on CERN's planned Future Circular Collider (FCC), a 91-kilometre tunnel that would run from Meyrin to near Annecy in France. The CO-CERNés Suisse collective, which includes the NGO Noé 21, the local sections of WWF and Patrimoine Suisse, and residents' associations, wants to amend the Geneva constitution so that voters have a say on the project. The organisers say their campaign is "not a fight against science, but against excess".
story.why: the FCC would be Europe's largest scientific infrastructure project, and Geneva voters could end up with a say on its construction on Swiss soil.
